tasks.short: Ask about symptoms and medicines, check the profile for interactions, compare products, advise on the choice and record the sale.

steps.what: Pharmacist asks the customer about symptoms, other medicines and conditions
Pharmacist checks the customer's medication profile for interactions with the product
Pharmacist looks up product information to compare medication brands and equipment
Pharmacist advises customers on the selection of a product
Pharmacist types the over-the-counter sale into the patient profile

tasks.design: Scanning the product at the counter runs the national interaction rules against the customer's profile in the pharmacy system ({OTHER}) and shows any warning to the pharmacist. A product view compares brands and devices by active ingredient, strength, price and reimbursement from the pharmacy's product file. With the customer's consent, the scanned sale is written to the profile. Asking and advising stay with the pharmacist.
tasks.previous_blocker: Interaction checks and product comparisons were looked up by hand at the counter.
tasks.enabler_now: Interaction rules and product files are already in pharmacy systems; linking them to the counter scan is configuration.
tasks.still_hard: Customers often do not want an over-the-counter sale recorded; then no check runs.
tasks.human_edge: Hearing that a customer's 'cold' sounds like something a doctor should see.

reach.learn: Whether counter checks raise warnings assistants would have missed.

evidence.claim: The G-Standaard checks interactions, contraindications, doses and duplicates; KNMP sets the content.
Recording an over-the-counter sale in a health profile needs the customer's consent; health data are special category.

assumptions: Boundary: from the customer's question to the recorded sale; prescription medicines are outside.
Input contract: medication profiles kept by the pharmacy system from dispensing; product file and interaction rules from the national drug database; fallback is manual lookup.
Asking and advising do not change.
Assistant time is outside the pharmacist's savings.
unknowns: Share of customers who consent to recording.
research_questions: How often does a counter check raise a relevant warning?

incremental.description: Pharmacist asks for consent to record the sale.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Customers who refuse recording save nothing on the check.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Measure activity, calculate decay and volume, draw up and measure doses, compare with the prescription and log results.

steps.what: Pharmacist assays radiopharmaceuticals in the dose calibrator
Pharmacist calculates disintegration over time and the volume to draw by hand
Pharmacist draws up and measures each patient dose
Pharmacist compares each measured dose with the prescription
Pharmacist writes measurements and doses in the logbook

tasks.design: Radiopharmacy software linked to the dose calibrator ({OTHER}) takes the measured activity, applies the decay formula for the isotope and the time of administration, and shows the volume to draw for each prescribed dose. After drawing, the measured dose is compared with the prescription within set tolerances for the pharmacist to confirm, and every measurement is logged without hand copying. Measuring and drawing up stay with the pharmacist.
tasks.previous_blocker: Decay and volumes were calculated by hand and results written in a logbook.
tasks.enabler_now: Dose calibrators export readings; decay correction is a fixed formula.
tasks.still_hard: Wrong isotope or time settings give wrong volumes; set-up must be checked.
tasks.human_edge: Noticing a reading that does not fit the batch.
tasks.altitude: The pharmacist confirms computed volumes and checks instead of calculating.

reach.learn: Whether logged doses cut transcription errors.

evidence.claim: Radiopharmacy software linked to dose calibrators computes decay correction and volumes and logs results.
Handling radioactive substances requires records under radiation protection rules.

assumptions: Boundary: from measuring the batch to the logged dose; administration is outside.
Input contract: dose prescriptions from the nuclear medicine physician; isotope data and tolerances set by the radiopharmacist; fallback is hand calculation.
Measuring and drawing do not change.
The software is validated before use.

incremental.description: Pharmacist validates the software after each update.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Radiopharmacies with existing dose software save less.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Select new meter users, invite them to a training slot, train them, check technique and first readings and note the training.

steps.what: Pharmacist selects patients starting a blood pressure or diabetes monitor for training
Pharmacist phones patients to invite them to a training slot
Patient agrees a training time with the pharmacy
Pharmacist trains people to use blood pressure devices or diabetes monitors
Pharmacist checks the patient's technique and first readings
Pharmacist notes the training in the patient profile

tasks.design: The pharmacy system ({OTHER}) lists patients who were dispensed a first blood pressure monitor or glucose meter; the pharmacist confirms the list, and the system then texts each patient a link to book a training slot instead of phoning. A pick-list note records the training. Training and checking technique stay in person.
tasks.previous_blocker: New meter users were found by memory and invited by phone.
tasks.enabler_now: Dispensing data show first meters, and booking links by text message are simple to set up.
tasks.still_hard: Older patients may not book online; the pharmacist still phones some.
tasks.human_edge: Watching a patient's hands and seeing why the readings are off.

reach.learn: Whether booked trainings reach more new users.

evidence.claim: Pharmacy systems can list first dispensings of a product and send booking links by text message.
Texting patients about a dispensed device uses health data; the purpose must fit the care relationship.

assumptions: Boundary: from new meter users to the noted training; ongoing monitoring is outside.
Input contract: dispensing history recorded by the pharmacy system; training slots set by the pharmacist; fallback is phoning.
Training and checks do not change.
Patients' time is priced as customer time, not as the pharmacist's savings.
research_questions: Do more new users get trained?

incremental.description: Pharmacist phones patients who do not book.
Patients open the texted link and book a training slot themselves.

approvals.approved_version: The training list as confirmed by the pharmacist in s1; patients added later need a new confirmation.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Most of this task is training in person.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Load the monthly drug database update, fix conflicting local records, find and merge duplicate patients, report errors to the supplier and test after software updates.

steps.what: Pharmacist loads the monthly drug update into the pharmacy databases and checks what changed
Pharmacist corrects local product and price records that conflict with the update
Pharmacist searches for duplicate or incomplete patient records
Pharmacist merges duplicate patient records after checking they are the same person
Pharmacist troubleshoots system errors with the software supplier by phone and e-mail
Pharmacist tests local settings after each software update

tasks.design: After each monthly update, the pharmacy system ({OTHER}) produces a change report limited to products the pharmacy stocks or dispenses, and rule checks list local product and price records that now conflict. Nightly data-quality rules list possible duplicate patients and missing fields. The pharmacist reviews and fixes the lists; merging, supplier contact and testing after updates stay manual.
tasks.previous_blocker: Changes and data errors were found by searching and by chance at the counter.
tasks.enabler_now: Update files are structured, and duplicate and completeness rules are plain code.
tasks.still_hard: Deciding whether two records are the same person needs care; a wrong merge mixes medication histories.
tasks.human_edge: Recognising that two near-identical records belong to twins.
tasks.altitude: The pharmacist works from lists instead of searching.

reach.learn: Whether completeness rules reduce later fixes.

evidence.claim: Duplicate and completeness rules for patient records are plain code.
The inspectorate names medication errors from wrong registration among the risks providers must manage.

assumptions: Boundary: from updates and errors to clean records; software development is outside.
Input contract: monthly drug update from the national drug database publisher; software updates from the pharmacy system supplier; fallback is manual searching.
Merging, supplier contact and testing do not change.
Supplier time is outside the pharmacist's savings.
Input contract for s3: patient records registered by assistants at the counter as today; the nightly rules read them and need no new entry.
research_questions: Do data errors found at the counter fall?

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Small pharmacies have few conflicts per update.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The pharmacist keeps advice, dosing checks, training and data judgements; lookups, calculations, invitations and searches go.
role.ambitious_version: A pharmacist whose records stay clean without weekend searches.
